event: VXE 897 aborted the VTOL launch three times in a row with the same error during a post-update SCO flight on the Jennings GCS (firmware 6.6.1); no damage.
component: Jennings GCS launch altitude request versus autopilot climb limit (legacy altitude request too high abort)
failure_mode: launch altitude request, with a ground altitude reference offset added, exceeded the autopilot climb limit plus margin, so the autopilot aborted the launch
contributing: first flight of this GCS laptop with 6.6.1 (earlier flights on 6.5.0)
GCS reported 400 ft although operator commanded a 200 ft transition

evidence.quote: I Just need to know if its the same issue, why it reported 400 ft even though operator commanded 200 ft transition
legacy bug rarely observed. updated aircraft to OGCS and did not experience issue
rare altitude bug not often observed, closing due to aircraft being updated with ogcs and having a successful flight.
namely a slightly negative reported AGL on the ground is additive to the launch altitude goal, which exceeds the climb limit + margin in the autopilot.
Investigation shows there is a 20-25ft delta in prelaunch altitude between the aircraft sensors and software (DTED + aircraft calibration).

team_view_in_comments: legacy bug rarely observed. updated aircraft to OGCS and did not experience issue

would_settle_it.what: the abort message text (for example 'Altitude request too high, launch aborted') and the requested versus reference altitude at each of the three launches
the launch and transition altitudes stored in the mission file

reasoning: The ticket never states the abort message, but engineers called it the known rare altitude bug and the aircraft flew fine once moved to OGCS. The linked VXEP-1290 and MS-384 describe the same repeatable launch abort caused by the ground altitude offset being added to the launch altitude request until it exceeds the autopilot climb limit. That points to the legacy GCS altitude handling, but no log text on this ticket confirms the same message, so it stays narrowed at low confidence.
notes: No Root Cause field; the closing text is in the Corrective Action field. Pack archives and the .vmis file were not converted, so the error message itself was not seen.

event: VXE 1021 (VXE35, OGCS) recognized its dropper pylons on the ground but would not arm them; it launched, OGCS showed armed alerts near the drop waypoint but nothing armed or dropped.
component: dropper pylon (WUP) detection and address assignment on the aircraft network
failure_mode: no ADVERT address assignment sent to either dropper, so the droppers were never armed
contributing: dropper configuration procedure unclear to operators (Ethernet versus serial WUP, XCOMM webpage enable after launch wizard resets)
possible IP or MAC address conflict with the gimbal on the aircraft network (under test)
separate: back left boom motor did not spin in launch wizard later the same day

evidence.quote: In the above test for this Ticket I do not see any detection of WUPs
From 1021 I never see an ADVERT sent to either Dropper for Address assignment. Something is very wrong there.
Reviewed with @John Clark does not appear to show any discrepancies.
Later on when they were wrapping 1021 up, the back left boom did not spin when commanded during launch wizard.

would_settle_it.what: whether the droppers request and receive a DHCP address in the .100 to .119 pool and whether ADVERTs are sent
XCOMM event log entries for pylon detection, ADVERT and arm commands
bench test of the WUP and both droppers on a known good aircraft

reasoning: The engineer reviewing the logs saw no WUP detection and no ADVERT address assignment to either dropper from 1021, so the droppers were never set up to arm. A later log review with the same engineer found no discrepancy, and the unit was shipped to SLO without a stated finding. This narrows the problem to the dropper/WUP detection chain but not to a part.
notes: Comments conflict: one says pylons were not detected at all, another confirms arm commands at lines 195 and 206 of a VSM event log. Back left boom did not spin in launch wizard later; 'back left boom' is not mapped to a motor number because a boom carries two motors, and it was not investigated on this ticket. Companion ticket VXEP-1984 covers the same droppers on 1039.

event: Droppers moved from VXE 1021 to VXE 1039 (VXE35, OGCS): the right pylon was detected and dropped correctly but the left pylon was never detected through repeated resets and power cycles.
component: left dropper pylon (WUP dropper) or its detection
failure_mode: left dropper never detected by firmware (ADVERT sent, no response), so it could not be armed
contributing: same left dropper may never have been verified working
manual configuration steps for B35 droppers not clearly documented for operators

evidence.quote: it detected the right pylon and activated it correctly, but it did not ever see the left, even through multiple autopilot resets and power cycles
This suggests that the Lefthand, Port Dropper has not been detected.
The falure could be hardware related. But the firmware does not see the Pylon.
have previously noted I have no output files I have reviewed where that particular dropper was working.

would_settle_it.what: XCOMM log ADVERT traffic and any reply from the left dropper
bench test of the left dropper and its harness and connector on a known good pylon port

reasoning: On 1039 the right pylon armed and dropped while ADVERTs went out with no left dropper ever answering, and the engineer said the fault could be hardware because the firmware does not see that pylon. The same left dropper had no record of ever working. That narrows the fault to the left dropper or its connection, without a confirmed part.
notes: Pylon 2 is the right hand (starboard) pylon per the comments, so the undetected one is pylon 1 (left, port). Equipment shipped to SLO with no finding recorded yet.

event: VXE 918 (Adv Nav, CHAOS payload) lost comms for about 8 minutes during a CHAOS development flight and never flew its lost comms plan; it was recovered and landed normally.
failure_mode: Arbitrator had no multi-aircraft filtering and never released control, so a ground station was always in control and the lost comms contingency never triggered
contributing: customer powered a second aircraft on the ground on the same network
ground radio frequency change caused the link loss and networked the two aircraft
customer contingency test procedures did not cover multi-aircraft operation

evidence.quote: According to the logs there was a connected GCS (CHAOS or OGCS) actively in control of the vehicle at all times, the system was behaving as designed.
The customer turned on another aircraft while on the ground.
Due to the lack of filtering in Arbitrator, Arbitrator never released the aircraft and the Stalker never conducted its lost comms contingencies.

team_view_in_comments: This was resolved by the customer to be an issue with their CUCS system (Arbitrator).
reasoning: Logs showed a ground station in control of the aircraft the whole time, so the aircraft correctly never entered lost comms. The customer traced it to their Arbitrator software, which lacked filtering for multiple aircraft and never released control after a second aircraft was powered and a frequency change networked them. The aircraft and VSM behaved as designed.
notes: No Root Cause field; the closing comment calls it operator error. The conclusion rests on the customer's finding as relayed in comments, so confidence is medium.

event: VXE 1016 (Adv Nav, main battery) got a low energy warning about 14 km out at 2000 ft with about 2 hours of displayed endurance and returned to base, landing with about 75 minutes displayed (about 30% SoC).
component: high winds (up to 60 fps aloft) driving high power draw; GCS endurance remaining estimate
failure_mode: energy use in high wind outpaced the displayed endurance estimate; autopilot low energy RTB triggered as designed
contributing: operated at or beyond published wind limits
GCS endurance remaining estimate does not adapt to high power draw
dash mode toggling in orbit to keep positive ground speed

evidence.quote: During cruise, AP indicated up to 60fps of wind (60fps = 40.9mph). On the ground the IAS was jumping from 20fps up to 32fps (32fps =21.8mph).
Average power throughout the flight was closing in on 700W, which is high but not abnormal based on high winds aloft.
I see nearly 60fps of wind during this flight with apvlife trending accordingly and landing with ~30% SoC.
I think one could certainly argue that the estimated endurance remaining is pretty poor.
GPS was available for this entire flight, so the issue present in Churchill was not here.

team_root_cause: Operator flying outside of wind limits. Battery endurance estimates not accurate in those conditions.
reasoning: Logs showed winds up to 60 fps aloft and average power near 700 W, with the autopilot energy estimate trending down and the aircraft landing at about 30% SoC. The low energy RTB worked as designed on a real energy shortfall, while the GCS endurance display overstated what was left. A GPS fault like the Churchill case was ruled out, and no voltage dropout was seen, so the battery itself is not implicated.
notes: Designed abort: scored on the degraded input (high wind energy use). Linked VXEP-1557 and VXEP-1865 (VXE 930) concern a different voltage dropout issue and were not read.

event: VXE 1014 (Adv Nav, OGCS 1.4.2) transitioned to VTOL below 50 ft AGL during landing, failed to arrest its descent and flew into a tree, damaging both booms, wingtips and the center wing.
component: OGCS 1.4.2 launch wizard landing altitude entry field
failure_mode: editing a 300 ft altitude to 200 ft could coerce the field to 2 ft, so transition occurred far too low; an autopilot altitude estimation error remains the alternative
contributing: operator moving quickly through launch wizard steps
possible airdata board v3001 altitude estimation error after long climbs or descents
unexplained apparent stall during fixed-wing flight (said unrelated)

evidence.quote: The most likely workflow that caused this was probably an attempt to edit 300 and make it 200
If you were to select and delete the 3 in 300 the value is immediately parsed/coerced so the text turns into 0 rather than 00.
Identified altitude estimation error that caused vehicle to transition at <50' AGL.
Operator states that RF motor did not engage after passing IP5.
After relaying findings from 1014 issue involving plz alttitude changing during mission planning, operator attempted to fly again

team_root_cause: Root cause appears to be altitude estimation error resulting in transition occurring at <50' AGL.  Investigating if known issue with airdata board is the culprit of the altitude estimation error.
disagreement: The Root Cause field blames an altitude estimation error, possibly the airdata board, but the later comment from the software lead says "The most likely workflow that caused this was probably an attempt to edit 300 and make it 200", which yields 2 ft because the OGCS 1.4.2 field coerces the value. The ticket title and the follow-on ticket VXEP-2006 ("plz alttitude changing during mission planning") follow the entry-error view, so the low transition more likely started at the OGCS entry than in the air data estimate.

would_settle_it.what: the landing pattern altitudes uploaded to the aircraft (2 ft versus 200 ft) and the estimated versus true altitude at transition
crash photos, and which airdata board version is installed

attachments_read: 64484_CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form V1014.pdf.md
reasoning: Engineers found the aircraft transitioned below 50 ft AGL, which explains hitting the tree. The software lead then showed how OGCS 1.4.2 turns an edit of 300 ft into 2 ft and said this was the most likely cause, fixed in 1.4.3 and 1.4.4, while the Root Cause field still points at an altitude estimation error from the airdata board. Neither is confirmed in the exported files, so the result is narrowed to the altitude used at transition with the OGCS entry the more likely start.
notes: Operator claimed the RF (motor 2, front right) motor did not engage; nothing in the engineering review supports a motor fault, so no position is given. The attached frontend log is from a post-incident session on 2026-09-04 (logins, mission download) and shows only OGCS version 1.4.2. RMA-1103 intake PDF has no text; aircraft replaced by 1114.

event: VXE 932 fuselage flying with the VXE 933 center wing completed transition from VTOL to fixed-wing flight at about 200 ft, then fell and crashed, destroying the aircraft.
failure_mode: airspeed reading erratic before takeoff and dropped to 0 shortly after transition, triggering fixed-wing low-airspeed landed-detection logic
contributing: launch wizard sensor faults that cleared only after about an hour of power cycling
mismatched fuselage and center wing assembled by error
logs end abruptly after the event, possible power loss not ruled out

evidence.quote: it looks to me like an airspeed sensor issue.  The airspeed measurement is varying pretty wildly during preflight, and then shortly after transition the airspeed measurement goes to 0.
There is some logic in fixed-wing that will detect landing if the airspeed is too low, it looks like this triggered:
From the logs, looks like FWD motor appropriately responded to throttle commands.
Over 6hrs of runtime on IB without replication of issue (both with and without incident VTOL AP).
All attempts to recreate the issue have failed thus far.

team_view_in_comments: it looked to me like an issue with the air data sensor, it was varying wildly on the ground and then went to 0 shortly after transition triggering the ‘landed’ logic.

would_settle_it.what: airspeed trace before takeoff and its drop to 0 after transition
XCL00138 and VTL00079 airspeed, landed-detection and power channels at the end of the log
bench test results on the incident air data and VTOL AP hardware

would_settle_it.file: air data pod and pitot of 933 center wing / 932 nose
would_settle_it.what: blockage, damage or connector fault in the airspeed sensor path

reasoning: Log review showed airspeed swinging wildly on the ground and dropping to 0 just after transition, which tripped the fixed-wing landed-detection logic, while the forward motor and battery looked healthy. Over six hours of bench running failed to reproduce anything, and one engineer suspects a power loss because the logs stop abruptly. The best supported reading is an air data (airspeed) fault, but it is not confirmed to a part.
notes: Fuselage 932 with center wing 933, mismatched by mistake. The nose was destroyed (data pulled using a slaved nose cone). RMA-1102 attachments are forms and image-only intake pages with no findings. Linked VXEP-1774 (VXE 933 sensor failure error) was not read; it may bear on the 933 center wing history.

event: VXE 966 (Adv Nav, E140 MWIR) had an apparent MCM reset after the operator power cycled the MWIR payload in flight, then climbed uncommanded to about 3800 ft AGL on a loiter command until U-drive brought it down and it landed.
component: MCM power path (TPS16630 eFuse on non-critical payload bus) and loiter altitude handling without reference altitude
failure_mode: payload power cycle reset the MCM, clearing the reference altitude; later loiter commands sent as MSL were read by the autopilot as AGL (about 4900 ft too high), causing a sustained climb
contributing: operator power cycled AUX payload power in flight to recover the gimbal
OGCS allows loiter commands when reference altitude is not set
mission uploads not supported after in-flight MCM reset

evidence.quote: Power cycled the MWIR and had a potential MCM brown out. Lost all mission elements and commanded a loiter here multiple times.
Since reference altitude was not set, the command essentially gets sent as an MSL command but gets interpreted by the autopilot as an AGL command.
In this case the MSL of the takeoff point was ~4900ft.
Resulting back-fed inrushcurrent tripping the fast-tripcomparator on the TPS16630Efuse (max 45A)
Payloads Affected: E140 regular before interface board, MWIR, E95.

team_view_in_comments: we believe what happened with the high altitude command is that the loiter commands are allowed when the reference altitude is not set.

would_settle_it.what: MCM restart time against the AUX power command, and the avionics box revision (Rev G or earlier)

reasoning: The log review shows the climb came from loiter commands sent while the reference altitude was unset, so an MSL value was flown as AGL with a 4900 ft takeoff elevation added. The reference altitude was lost because the MCM reset after the MWIR was power cycled, which matches the systemic mechanism in VXEP-1315 where payload inrush trips the MCM eFuse. The climb mechanism is shown in the logs; the eFuse trip on this aircraft is by match to the parent ticket, so confidence is medium.
notes: Plan and Issue Status fields only link to VXEP-1315. Tail written as 'XVE 966' in the tail field. Linked VXEP-1890, VXEP-1956 and MS-1684 were not read; they are other cases and the software follow-up of the same issue.

event: VXE 1013 (Adv Nav) was reported to pitch down and drop to about 50 ft AGL short of the PLZ during landing and touch down off the pad; the downloaded data show a normal transition and an operator nudge back toward the launch point.
component: operator manual nudge during VTOL landing descent
failure_mode: aircraft nudged by operators away from the commanded landing point; reported altitude drop not seen in the data
contributing: possible confusion over which landing pattern was active (straight-in uploaded, then a left turn pattern)
possible tailwind landing
AAR may not be the incident flight

evidence.quote: I can confirm that all landing patterns were set correctly with a pattern altitude of 200ft
Thanks for the writeup, this does not match what I see in the data.
this flight looks like a nominal transition and then a landing nudge back to the launch point.
I doubt that the large altitude loss being reported was due to a tail wind unless it was extreme

would_settle_it.what: the aggressive nudge near 2:40 and the altitude during the landing approach
confirm whether the AAR is the incident flight and whether any pitch down to 50 ft occurred

reasoning: Engineers confirmed the landing patterns were correctly set at 200 ft, and the autopilot logs and OGCS replay show a normal transition with operators nudging the aircraft during descent. The reported pitch down to 50 ft is not in the data, and the aircraft later flew normally. No aircraft fault was found; the event traces to operator handling.
notes: Raised as a repeat of the VXEP-1988 (1014) low transition, but the data do not show that behavior. A setpoint discrepancy (200 ft VTOL versus 300 ft fixed wing) during transition was noted but not followed up.
